samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers state the ask on the first slide, show fairly that Option B's +26% falls short of the roughly 30% needed, and flag the same missing figures: Dunmore's capacity, its running cost and what the 26% is measured against. A's titles all state conclusions, and its spoken script briefly explains both 'commissary' and 'utilization'. B uses some topic-style titles ('Build a third kitchen, or run Eastside longer', 'Decision requested today'), never defines utilization, and adds small unsupported claims such as Dunmore landing 'ahead of the third new cafe'. B's gap list and risk slide are more thorough, but A is tighter and fits the rubric better. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers open with the ask, show fairly that Option B's +26% falls short of the ~30% needed, and flag the same key gaps: Dunmore's capacity, what the 26% is measured against, and Dunmore's running costs. B's titles all state conclusions, and it defines both commissary and utilization in a sentence each; A's slide 5 title is closer to a topic label, and A never explicitly defines utilization. B loses a little on item 4: it annualizes the declined orders into a run-rate (though it labels this) and adds assumed calendar dates, while A's extra figures are all plain arithmetic on the supplied facts.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A is better overall. Every A slide title states a conclusion, so reading the titles alone tells the whole argument, and each slide carries one idea, with the speaker notes kept separate. B handles Option B, the explanations for non-food members and the list of gaps to close just as well, but several of its titles are topic labels ('Title', 'The ask', 'Two options') and some slides pack in more than one idea. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B's slide titles are conclusions, so reading them in order tells the whole argument. A uses topic labels like 'Title', 'The ask' and 'Two options', and its slide 6 packs in several ideas. Both put the ask up front, show that +26% falls short of 30%, and stick to the supplied numbers. B makes one slip: it says a +26% that applies only to Eastside would make the shortfall smaller, when it would actually be larger. A gets this right.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both decks put the ask first, keep spoken lines apart from slide content and fit 15 minutes. B treats Option B more fairly: it says outright that the second shift is cheaper and faster, shows it is about 4 points short of the 30% target, and adds a slide on how the business runs for the two non-food members. B goes beyond the facts in a few places, including the 'above roughly 90%' threshold and saying Dunmore gives 'room beyond 30%' when no capacity figure exists, though it flags that gap. A's titles read more cleanly as an argument. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers state the ask on slide 1, use titles that state conclusions, define commissary and utilization in plain terms, and show that +26% falls short of the 30% needed. A is slightly stronger: its A-vs-B table makes the trade-offs clear (B is about 4 points short), and its gap list and likely questions are more thorough. B says Dunmore gives 'a second site' when it would be the third kitchen, and both decks claim Dunmore covers the 30% without a capacity figure. A also adds an unsupported 'roughly 90%' threshold.

A uses a moment every hygienist will recognize, but it runs on as one long sentence and ends by announcing the topic ('today we're going to talk about...'). pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a single opening with no statistics and no preamble. B is stronger on item 3: it gets the room participating with a moment every hygienist knows, then turns the question on the audience, which sets up the talk's theme without stating it. A also opens with a concrete scene, but it ends by announcing the topic ('today I want to talk about why...'), which the rubric marks down. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both give a single opening with no stats or preamble. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a single spoken opening with no statistics and no preamble or closing offer. B describes a moment every hygienist knows, hearing 'every day' while looking at gums that say otherwise, and it does so cleanly. A's role reversal is clever but muddled: hygienists who really do floss daily would truthfully say so in the chair too, so the second hand-raise loses its point. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give one clean opening with no statistics and no preamble, so they meet the format rules equally. A is a clear, familiar moment every hygienist will recognize. B puts the audience in the patient's chair, so they feel why people shade the truth, which leads straight into the talk's 'why' question. That makes B the stronger hook, even though its wording is a little busier.
